title: Bessent Blames Lutnick for Letting China Acquire Nvidia Chips, PBS Reports
body:
Washington – In a sharply worded confrontation that has quickly become a flashpoint in the administration’s ongoing battle over China’s access to cutting‑edge technology, Treasury Deputy Secretary Scott Bessent publicly charged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick with negligence after a senior Nvidia engineer reportedly supplied the Chinese government with the company’s most advanced artificial‑intelligence chip designs. The allegation, made during a closed‑door briefing that was later leaked to the press, underscores the growing tension between two of President Donald Trump’s most influential economic advisers and raises fresh doubts about the effectiveness of U.S. export‑control policies.

Bessent’s criticism centers on the failure to enforce the “Entity List” restrictions that were tightened after Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was forced to step down amid a scandal involving alleged undisclosed ties to Chinese state‑owned firms. According to the Treasury official, the Commerce Department’s Office of Export Enforcement “did not act swiftly or decisively enough to block the transfer of critical design data” that could enable Beijing to accelerate its domestic AI chip program. Bessent warned that the lapse could erode the United States’ technological edge and compromise national security, urging “immediate corrective action” and a full review of the department’s oversight mechanisms.

Lutnick, who has overseen the Commerce Department’s export‑control regime since early 2025, responded in a brief statement that the agency “remains fully committed to protecting American innovation” and that “all appropriate investigative steps are already underway.” He declined to comment on the specifics of the Nvidia case, citing ongoing investigations, but emphasized that the department has “enhanced its inter‑agency coordination with Treasury, the Department of Defense, and intelligence partners” to prevent similar breaches. The exchange marks a rare public spat between two senior officials who have traditionally worked behind closed doors to shape the administration’s hard‑line stance on China.

The dispute emerges against a backdrop of escalating U.S.–China rivalry in the semiconductor arena. Since the Biden administration first imposed curbs on advanced chip exports in 2022, successive administrations have sought to tighten controls, arguing that AI‑driven chips are “dual‑use” technologies that could bolster China’s military capabilities. Nvidia, the world’s leading GPU maker, has been at the center of the controversy, with its A100 and newer H100 chips forming the backbone of high‑performance computing and deep‑learning workloads. The alleged leak of design schematics, if confirmed, would represent the most significant breach of export controls since the 2019 Huawei sanctions.

Industry analysts caution that the political infighting could have unintended consequences for the U.S. tech sector. “When senior officials start publicly blaming each other, it creates uncertainty for companies that are already navigating a complex regulatory landscape,” said Maya Patel, senior fellow at the Center for Technology Policy. “Companies may become overly cautious, delaying product rollouts or pulling investment, which could cede market share to rivals in Europe or Japan that face less regulatory turbulence.” Moreover, the episode may embolden Chinese firms to intensify espionage efforts, knowing that internal U.S. disagreements could create enforcement gaps.

Congressional oversight committees are expected to summon both Bessent and Lutnick for testimony in the coming weeks. Lawmakers from both parties have expressed concern that the current framework for safeguarding advanced semiconductor technology is “fragmented and under‑resourced.” A bipartisan group of senators has already introduced legislation to create a unified inter‑agency task force with expanded authority to audit and sanction foreign entities that attempt to acquire restricted U.S. tech.

As the administration grapples with the fallout, the episode serves as a stark reminder of the challenges inherent in policing a globally intertwined supply chain. The outcome of the internal review and any subsequent policy adjustments will likely shape the trajectory of U.S. technology leadership for years to come. If the Treasury and Commerce departments can reconcile their differences and reinforce export‑control mechanisms, they may yet preserve the strategic advantage that has long underpinned America’s dominance in AI and high‑performance computing. Failure to do so, however, could accelerate the very diffusion of capability that the United States has striven to contain.
